FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Understand the anatomy of the ankle syndesmosis and ligaments.
Recognize that a high index of suspicion often is necessary for diagnosis of syndesmotic
injuries.
Appreciate that syndesmotic injuries often are associated with other pathology.
Discuss the patient history, physical examination, and imaging study findings associated with
syndesmotic injuries.
Review the management of syndesmotic injuries, which varies from nonsurgical to surgical
management depending on the stability of the ankle mortise.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy

Overview
Definition/pathomechanics
The ankle syndesmosis is responsible for maintaining the relationship between the distal
fibula and tibia at the articulation with the talus.
A combination of dorsiflexion and external rotation forces results in syndesmotic injuries.
Severe injuries are associated with deltoid ligament disruption and fibular fracture.
Instability results in lateral and rotatory displacement of the talus.
Longer recuperation is expected in patients with these high ankle sprains/syndesmotic
injuries.

Overview
The ankle syndesmosis is continuous with the interosseous membrane proximally and is
located at the level of the tibial plafond. Several mechanisms may result in injury to the
syndesmosis. Dissimilar from most ankle sprains, in which injury to the lateral ligaments
occurs after an inversion mechanism of injury, syndesmotic sprains typically result from
eversion and external rotation forces. This scenario may occur if internal rotation of the
leg and body on a firmly planted foot causes an external rotatory force on the fibula. A
spectrum of severity may occur after injury to the syndesmotic complex, ranging from
subtle sprains to complete diastasis and instability.
Epidemiology
Often referred to as high ankle sprains
Syndesmosis injured in 1% to18% of all ankle sprains1

Epidemiology
The ligaments of the syndesmosis bear a great amount of force during sporting activities
and, therefore, are prone to injury. Syndesmotic sprains are common in collision sports,
such as football, in which an external rotatory force is sustained after direct impact to
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Syndesmotic Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000002
2/21

the ankle; however, injuries can occur via other mechanisms, such as shearing, torsion,
and hyperdorsiflexion. Injury to the complex may be associated with a fracture or may
be purely ligamentous. Injuries range from a minor grade I sprain to complete rupture of
the ligaments and diastasis of the distal tibiofibular joint. A syndesmotic injury requires
approximately twice as much recovery time before return to play as lateral ligament
injuries and, therefore, should be managed in a different manner.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The ankle syndesmosis is made up of four ligaments:
Anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (AITFL)
Posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (PITFL)
Inferior transverse ligament (ITL)
Interosseous ligament (IOL)
The AITFL contributes the most toward stability.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Although the distal tibia and fibula are congruent, most of the stability of the
syndesmosis comes from its ligamentous support, which includes the AITFL, PITFL, ITL,
and IOL, which span the distal tibia and fibula. The AITFL extends from the Chaput
tubercle on the anterolateral tibia to the Wagstaffe tubercle on the anterior edge of the
fibula. The PITFL extends from the Volkmann tubercle on the posterolateral edge of the
tibia to the posterior portion of the lateral malleolus. The ITFL is the fibrocartilaginous
distal extent of the PITFL, and the IOL comprises the thickened distal portion of the
interosseous membrane (Figure 1).

Figure 1 Anterolateral (A) and posterior (B) view schematic drawings show the ligaments
of the ankle syndesmosis. AITFL = anteroinferior tibiofibular ligament, ATFL = anterior
talofibular ligament, CFL = calcaneofibular ligament, PITFL = posteroinferior tibiofibular
ligament, PTFL = posterior talofibular ligament. (Reproduced with permission from
Williams BT, Ahrberg AB, Goldsmith MT, et al: Ankle syndesmosis: A qualitative and
quantitative anatomic analysis. Am J Sports Med 2015;43(1):88-97.)
The motion that occurs between the distal tibia and fibula is limited but includes an
increase in the intermalleolar distance of approximately 1.5 mm during ankle range of
motion. Rotational movement of approximately 12° to 17° also occurs in the horizontal
plane, with a mean of 2.4 mm of distal migration of the fibula.2 If these limits of motion
are overstressed by a force, the ligaments tear and/or the bone fractures.
The AITFL contributes the most to stability of the mortise, followed by the IOL, PITFL, and
ITL.3
Classification
Useful to classify injuries as stable or unstable


Classification
The West Point Ankle Grading System is a classification system designed to guide
management. Grade I injuries are mild sprains/tearing of the AITFL and, therefore, are
not associated with syndesmotic instability. Grade II injuries consist of a torn AITFL and
partial tear of the IOL, with instability observed. Grade III injuries involve tearing of all
four ligaments (AITFL, PITFL, IOL, ITL) and are associated with definite instability.
Whether an injury is stable or unstable is the most important factor to guide
management.4 In determining the severity of the injury, clinicians must assess for injury
to the deltoid ligament.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Direct contact or external rotation mechanism of injury

Patient History
A high index of suspicion is required in evaluating syndesmotic injuries because of the
considerable disability that may result, especially in athletes. Obtaining an accurate
patient history is critical in diagnosing syndesmotic injury. The patient should describe
the mechanism of injury and even demonstrate the mechanism of injury on the
contralateral side, if able. A video recording of the injury, if available, also may be helpful.
Suspect a high ankle sprain if the patient describes the ankle as having turned or rotated
outward rather than inward. In patients with a lateral ankle sprain after an inversion
injury, pain tends to be localized along the lateral ankle. Conversely, in patients with a
high ankle sprain, pain may be reported in the medial ankle and/or more proximally
along the anterolateral leg.5
Physical Examination
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Syndesmotic Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000002
5/21

If instability is present, the patient usually cannot bear weight.
Tenderness near the syndesmosis and deltoid ligaments
Provocative tests
Squeeze test
External rotation test
Single limb standing test
Syndesmosis tape test

Physical Examination
Often, less swelling is present than that observed in patients with a lateral ankle
ligament injury, and local swelling and ecchymosis that exist after an acute injury may
quickly resolve and transition to diffuse signs and symptoms, making the diagnosis less
obvious. Ecchymosis proximal to the ankle joint and tenderness to palpation over the
anterior and posterior tibiofibular ligaments, the interosseous membrane, and/or the
interosseous ligament indicate syndesmotic injury.6
The practitioner should examine the patient in the sitting and prone positions. The knee
should be examined for stability because external rotation of the foot may cause a
valgus moment to the knee and subsequent medial collateral ligament injury. The
proximal fibula should be palpated for tenderness from a possible fracture that is
characteristically observed with a Maisonneuve injury. Clinicians should attempt to elicit
pain by palpating along the deltoid ligament medially. With the patient in the prone
position, with the feet suspended off the edge of the bed, a posterior to anterior
translational force on the distal fibula may exhibit syndesmotic pain and instability.
Several provocative tests are designed to detect syndesmotic injury and instability;
however, none has proven completely reliable. A useful diagnostic tool is the squeeze
test, in which the examiner squeezes the tibiofibular joint around the area of the midcalf
in a mediolateral compression. Patients with a positive squeeze test will experience pain
distal to the point of compression. Pain at the syndesmosis with the maneuver strongly
suggests a syndesmotic injury.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Syndesmotic Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000002
6/21

Similarly, the external rotation test is helpful, and, if positive, may indicate a prolonged
recovery compared with that associated with a lateral ankle sprain.7 The external
rotation test is performed with the patient sitting, with knees flexed 90° off the edge of
the bed. The ankle is placed in neutral dorsiflexion, and an external rotation force is
applied. Reproduction of pain at the syndesmosis indicates a positive test.
Other provocative tests include assessing whether the patient can rise and stand on the
ball of the injured foot. A single limb standing stress test assesses whether the patient
can stand on the affected limb and rotate his/her pelvis to the contralateral side,
producing an external rotation force at the ankle.
The syndesmotic tape test is another useful examination for patients with subtle or
chronic instability. The patient is asked to perform a single heel rise on the affected limb.
If this reproduces pain about the syndesmosis, the next step is to wrap medical tape
circumferentially around the leg, just proximal to the malleoli, and then repeat the single
limb heel rise. Improvement in syndesmotic pain after taping should increase suspicion
of a chronic or subtle syndesmotic injury.
Imaging
Radiography
Plain radiography
AP views may demonstrate decreased tibiofibular overlap.
Mortise views may demonstrate increased tibiofibular clear space.
Tibial radiographs should be obtained to rule out a proximal fibula fracture (Maisonneuve
fracture).
In subtle cases, the diagnosis is confirmed via weight-bearing radiographs and stress
radiographs (in eversion and external rotation), with comparison with the opposite side.

Radiography
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Syndesmotic Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000002
7/21

Although the physical examination is a useful tool for assessing syndesmotic injury,
imaging studies are more diagnostic. The radiographic evaluation of a suspected
syndesmotic injury begins with the standard three ankle views, preferably ordered as
weight-bearing views. All views are assessed for signs of syndesmotic widening and/or
possible avulsion fractures.
On AP radiographs, tibiofibular overlap should be at least 5 mm. Clinicians may suspect
syndesmotic injury if decreased tibiofibular overlap is observed. On mortise views,
tibiofibular clear space typically is less than 5 mm. More than 6 mm of widening of the
tibiofibular clear space indicates syndesmotic disruption. Full-length tibia/fibula
radiographs also should be obtained to rule out a proximal fibula fracture, which may be
observed in patients with a Maisonneuve injury.5
If findings on static radiographs appear normal but a high suspicion for a syndesmotic
injury exists, then an external rotation stress view can be obtained (Figure 2). Stressing
the ankle in this fashion may generate pain and may require the administration of an
anesthetic agent. The view is obtained by applying an external rotation and abduction
force to the ankle while a mortise radiograph is obtained. Any increased tibiofibular clear
space or decreased overlap suggests a syndesmotic disruption. Note that the fibula
translates posteriorly to a greater extent than laterally with external rotation stress;
however, the difficulty in interpreting a sagittal ankle radiograph under stress makes
coronal imaging more consistent. Bilateral weight-bearing radiographs also may be
helpful to compare the amount of tibiofibular clear space between the two sides.

Figure 2 Fluoroscopic images of the ankle of a patient with a syndesmotic sprain. A,
Static image shows no displacement. B, External rotation stress image obtained with the
patient under anesthesia shows mortise and syndesmotic instability. C, Image obtained
after stabilization with the use of syndesmotic screws. (Reproduced from Lin J: Sports-
related injuries of the foot and ankle, in Chou, LB: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Foot
and Ankle, ed 6. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp
393-408.)
Computed Tomography
CT may help evaluate the syndesmotic space, especially in chronic or subtle cases.

Computed Tomography
Additional imaging is indicated if plain radiographs are inconclusive but suspicion for a
high ankle sprain remains high. Axial weight-bearing CT scans of bilateral ankles allow
for side-to-side comparison and may reveal even small amounts of widening or
incongruity of the tibiofibular articulation.5
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may show subtle syndesmotic ligament injury.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRIs may be diagnostic if plain radiographs are inconclusive. Although MRI is a static
imaging modality and does not allow for assessment of dynamic instability, it may reveal
structural injury to the anterior tibiofibular ligament8 (Figure 3) and to the posterior
syndesmotic ligaments and posterior malleolus. Axial MRIs often are the most useful in
diagnosing acute injury to the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis. In patients with a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Syndesmotic Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000002
9/21

syndesmotic injury, fluid-sensitive axial MRIs may reveal edema within the interosseous
membrane.5 In addition, MRI is useful in identifying associated pathology.
Figure 3 Axial MRI of a right ankle shows an anterior tibiofibular ligament tear. (Courtesy
of Christopher Kreulen, MD, MS; Eric Giza, MD; and Erin Haggerty, MD, Sacramento, CA.)
Differential Diagnosis
Lateral ankle sprain
Medial ankle sprain
Ankle fracture
Maisonneuve fracture

Differential Diagnosis
The differential diagnosis includes lateral ankle sprains, medial ankle sprains, ankle
fractures, and Maisonneuve fractures. A thorough patient history and precise physical
examination usually will reveal an injury of the syndesmosis.
Management
Highly dependent on the stability of the syndesmotic complex
Stable injuries (grade I and II) managed nonsurgically
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000002
10/21

Unstable injuries (unstable grade II, grade III) require surgical management.

Management
Individualizing treatment will yield the best outcomes. Grade I injuries in which the AITFL
is torn (or partially torn) but stability is maintained are best managed nonsurgically. For
grade II injuries, clinicians must determine the stability of the injury and the ankle.
Because grade II injuries may be stable or unstable, advanced imaging studies and
provocative tests are highly recommended. Concomitant deltoid ligament injury also
must be ruled out because this also may affect the stability of the ankle joint. In
competitive athletes or active patients, surgical treatment may allow for more rapid
return to sports activity or other desired activities. Surgical treatment is indicated in
patients with obvious diastasis observed on plain or stress radiographs (Figure 4) and
patients in whom rehabilitation fails.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM

Figure 4 AP ankle radiograph demonstrates a type IV syndesmotic injury. (Reproduced
with permission from Clanton TO, Waldrop NE: Athletic injuries to the soft tissues of the
foot and ankle, in Coughlin MJ, Saltzman CL, Anderson RB, eds: Mann’s Surgery of the Foot
and Ankle, ed 9. Philadelphia, PA, Mosby Elsevier, 2014, pp 1531-1687.)
Nonsurgical Management
Indicated for stable injuries (grade I and most grade II)
Initial management consists of a period of rest, ice, compression, and elevation and
immobilization.
Recovery tends to be prolonged (twice that of a standard ankle sprain).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM


Nonsurgical Management
In patients with a grade I injuries or grade II injuries in whom nonsurgical treatment is
appropriate, management is similar to that for lateral ankle sprains with several key
differences. A combination of rest, ice, compression, and elevation and a period of
immobilization and non–weight bearing is the initial treatment protocol. Because pain
and swelling often are more severe and weight bearing takes longer to reestablish after
a high ankle sprain than after a lateral ankle sprain, immobilization may be for as long as
4 to 6 weeks5 A controlled ankle motion boot and crutches often are appropriate for 2
weeks; the controlled ankle motion boot may be replaced by a stirrup brace after the
patient is no longer tender at the syndesmotic complex.
After the initial inflammation and swelling have subsided, a rehabilitation regimen for
range of motion, strengthening, and eventually functional exercises is instituted.
Return to sports participation may be twice that of a lateral ankle sprain. Therefore, early
patient counseling is important. Often, patients must avoid sports activity for 4 to 8
weeks. A systematic review reported that time lost from sports after a high ankle sprain
ranged from 0 to 137 days and that the mean time lost from sports ranged from 10 to 52
days.9
Surgical Management
Unstable grade II and grade III injuries observed on MRI and positive provocative tests or
diastasis observed on plain or stress radiographs require surgical stabilization.
High-level athletes or active patients with subtle diastasis or a tear of the syndesmotic
ligaments may benefit from surgical stabilization.
Screws and/or suture-button fixation may be used for stabilization.
The optimal fixation construct (screw versus suture-button fixation, screw size, number of
cortices engaged, and need for screw removal) is controversial.
Surgical management is followed by functional rehabilitation.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Syndesmotic Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000002
13/21


Surgical Management
Grade III syndesmotic injuries are unstable and require surgical management. Surgical
stabilization has been performed with the use of a solid metal transyndesmotic screw or
screws. Recently, the advent of suture-button stabilization has led to alternative
stabilization of the syndesmosis. Controversy exists with regard to whether screw
fixation and/or suture-button fixation is the optimal treatment option. Regardless of the
fixation construct, arthroscopic assessment of the ankle joint may be helpful (Figure 5) .
The surgeon can evaluate for chondral defects, visualize the deltoid (with and without
valgus stress), and débride the syndesmosis of inflamed tissue and scarring to eliminate
soft-tissue blocking reduction or the widened joint. After arthroscopic joint débridement,
the syndesmosis is stabilized with the use of a screw or suture-button construct.
Figure 5 Arthroscopic images of an ankle show evaluation of an ankle fracture with
syndesmotic disruption. A, Reduction of the syndesmosis is confirmed before (left) and
after (right) syndesmotic screw fixation. B, Syndesmotic disruption with disruption of the
Mercedes sign (left) is observed before the syndesmosis is anatomically reduced and the
Mercedes sign is restored (right) (Reproduced from Ferkel EI, Ruland CL: Arthroscopy of
the foot and ankle and osteochondral lesions of the talus, in Chou LB, ed: Orthopaedic
Knowledge Update: Foot and Ankle, ed 7. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2025, pp 403-426.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Syndesmotic Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000002
14/21

Appropriate reduction of the syndesmosis is essential before fixation. A large reduction
clamp may help compress the tibia and fibula together to reduce the joint. The tines of
the forceps should be placed in the proper orientation so the syndesmosis is reduced
along the proper axis of slight external rotation. This can be accomplished by positioning
the clamp along the posterolateral edge of the fibula and the anteromedial portion of
the tibia. Because of the shape of the talus (more widened anterior than posterior), the
forceps also should be positioned with the ankle in neutral dorsiflexion. Excessive
dorsiflexion may lead to increased external rotation and lateral translation of the fibula9
and, therefore, should be avoided. Fixation of the ankle in excessive plantar flexion may
lead to inability to fully dorsiflex the ankle. Appropriate reduction should be verified via
fluoroscopy and/or arthroscopy before fixation.
For screw fixation, a drill hole should be made under fluoroscopic guidance parallel to
the joint approximately 1.5 to 2 cm above the tibial plafond. The direction of the drill
hole should be parallel to that of the reduction forceps oriented from posterolateral to
anteromedial. Screws may be placed through the near cortex in isolation or through
both cortices of the tibia. The number of cortices requiring engagement remains
controversial. A screw positioned just through the near cortex of the tibia avoids a
prominent and potentially irritable screw tip penetrating through the medial tibial
cortex. Fixation of the screw in both cortices of the tibia may prevent screw pull-out and
fixation failure, especially in osteoporotic bone. Screw size also remains controversial,
with most surgeons using 3.5-mm or 4.5-mm solid core screws. If a second screw is used
for fixation, it should be positioned approximately 1 cm parallel and proximal to the first
screw. Occasionally, a one-third tubular plate is used to add strength to the construct,
even if the fibula is not fractured. Typically, screws are removed 3 to 4 months
postoperatively; however, the need for screw removal also is controversial.
A nonabsorbable suture-button device has several theoretic advantages over screw
fixation. One advantage is that the suture-button device provides more flexible fixation
and helps restore normal tibiofibular joint mechanics without the need for subsequent
screw removal or the potential for screw breakage.10A study reported a decrease in
syndesmotic malreduction with suture-button fixation compared with screw fixation.11
Similar to screw fixation, suture-button fixation requires precise joint reduction and

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000002
15/21

orientation of fixation. Occasionally, two suture buttons can be used, and in larger
athletes, placement of the buttons through a buttress plate may add stability. In
addition, a screw and a suture button can be combined.
Recent studies support augmentation of the AITFL with the use of nonabsorbable suture
tape to further reduce external rotation instability in patients with a syndesmotic injury.
This is recommended in athletes and patients with general ligamentous laxity.
Intraoperatively, a suture anchor loaded with suture tape is inserted to the AITFL
insertion at the anteromedial corner of the fibula (Wagstaff tubercle). This suture tape is
then fixed under appropriate tension with another anchor device to the AITFL origin at
the anterolateral corner of the tibia (Chaput tubercle). This simulates the AITFL
anatomically and further reduces anterior syndesmotic instability via a closing-book
phenomenon. The remnant of the AITFL, which often is torn off the Chaput tubercle also
is repaired with the use of another suture anchor on the tibial side.
Lastly, the deltoid ligament must be repaired if instability still exists because an anterior
deltoid ligament tear often accompanies syndesmotic disruption in patients with a
dorsiflexion and external rotation type of injury. Assessment is performed after
syndesmotic reduction and fixation (with or without augmentation of the AITFL). Under
fluoroscopic guidance with the ankle dorsiflexed, if the medial clear space widens with
external rotation and valgus stress, deltoid ligament repair is necessary. The repair is
focused on the tibionavicular ligament and the tibiospring ligament. For the incision, the
anteromedial portal of the ankle arthroscope can be extended distally to expose the
anterior portion of the deltoid ligament for appropriate repair.
Postoperative Management
Non–weight bearing for 6 weeks postoperatively
Functional rehabilitation
Screw removal 3 to 4 months postoperatively, if required

Postoperative Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Syndesmotic Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000002
16/21

A 6- to 12-week period of protected weight bearing is required to allow the ligaments to
heal after high-grade syndesmotic injuries. In general, patients can be transitioned to a
removable boot 2 weeks postoperatively to begin working on range of motion.
Functional rehabilitation is subsequently initiated. After strength is equivalent to that of
the contralateral side and the patient has confidence to make cutting movements, they
may return to sports practice.
Typically, syndesmotic screws are left in place for 3 to 4 months postoperatively. Screw
removal remains controversial. Screw removal requires a second trip to the operating
room and potential loss of reduction if ligament healing is incomplete. The disadvantage
of maintaining the screws includes potential restriction in ankle range of motion, screw
breakage, or osteolysis about the screws. Athletes may be allowed to complete their
athletic season, and screw removal performed after the athletic season is complete.
Chronic Syndesmotic Injuries
Diagnosis of a syndesmotic injury may be delayed, leading to a chronic problem.
Instability and soft-tissue impingement may cause ankle pain in patients with a chronic
syndesmosis injury.
Management varies and includes débridement, arthrodesis, stabilization via screw or flexible
fixation, and delayed reconstruction.

Chronic Syndesmotic Injuries
Diagnosis of an acute distal tibiofibular syndesmotic injury may be difficult, especially if
plain radiographs demonstrate a normal distal tibiofibular joint space. Injury of the
syndesmosis may be missed, leading to a chronic condition.3 Diagnosis of a chronic
syndesmosis injury may be more difficult because symptoms, physical examination
findings, and imaging studies vary and may be less clear. In patients with an acute distal
tibiofibular syndesmotic injury, the external rotational stress and tibiofibular squeeze
tests are diagnostically helpful; however, in one study of 20 patients with a chronic distal
tibiofibular syndesmosis injury, only three patients had pain with the external rotation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Syndesmotic Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000002
17/21

stress test and only two patients had pain with the tibiofibular squeeze test,12
confirming limitations in the diagnosis of chronic injuries via physical examination alone.
Two causes of disability are associated with chronic syndesmotic injuries: instability and
impingement of hypertrophic soft tissue inside the distal tibiofibular joint.13 Imaging
studies, such as MRIs, may be more difficult to interpret given the chronicity of injury.
Diagnostic MRI criteria for chronic syndesmotic injuries include no visualization of the
syndesmosis ligaments, abnormal course, wavy or irregular contour, thickening of
ligaments, and increased signal intensity on T2- and T1-weighted MRIs.12 Occasionally, a
syndesmotic injury may have been overlooked during management of an associated
ankle fracture. In such instances, fibular length and rotation must be assessed. Similarly,
the posterior malleolus also must be carefully scrutinized in patients with a prior ankle
fracture. If injury to the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis is suspected and nonsurgical
management fails, arthroscopy may be necessary for diagnosis and management.13
No clear standard exists for management of chronic syndesmosis injuries. Arthroscopic
marginal resection of hypertrophic soft tissue within the ankle joint may help improve
pain and disability. Debate exists with regard to whether transcortical screw fixation or
flexible suspensory fixation should be performed to attain stability in patients who have
a chronic syndesmotic injuries with distal tibiofibular joint widening of 2 mm or more.
Fusion of the tibiofibular joint also has been proposed as a treatment option for chronic
injuries; however, fusion should be reserved for patients in whom severe arthrosis is
present within the joint. Augmentation of the AITFL may be beneficial because a
chronically torn AITFL often is not repairable;14 however, additional long-term
prospective studies are necessary to evaluate this treatment option for chronic
syndesmotic injuries.
Complications
Symptomatic hardware/hardware failure
Malreduction
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Syndesmotic Instability
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000002
18/21

Chronic instability
Ligament ossification/synostosis

Complications
Complications after syndesmotic surgery include complications typically ascribed to
orthopaedic surgery in general, such as infection, skin breakdown, and nerve injuries.
Complications specific and especially pertinent to syndesmotic fixation include
symptomatic hardware, hardware failure, malreduction, failed reduction with chronic
instability, ligament ossification, and synostosis. Symptomatic hardware, especially that
observed with four-cortex screw fixation, may require removal after soft-tissue healing is
complete. Maintenance of screws may result in screw breakage or osteolysis about the
screws. Broken screws may not cause any harm to the patient, and osteolysis does not
appear to result in poorer outcomes.13 Malreduction of the syndesmosis may occur and
is best assessed via postoperative CT scans. Ossification of the syndesmotic ligaments is
relatively rare; however, if symptomatic synostosis occurs, the synostosis can be
surgically resected.
Mark as Complete
Recommended Readings
